verdict.rationale: The noun kephale (G2776) is predicated of Christ in relation to the body and the ekklesia (G1577) five times across two letters: Eph 1:22 (God gave him, kephalen accusative, as head over all things to the church), Eph 4:15 (he kephale, Christos), Eph 5:23 (kephale of the church, predicate nominative anchored to Christos by name), Col 1:18 (autos estin he kephale of the body, the church), and Col 2:10 (he kephale of all rule and authority). Each predication uses a singular subject, and in Col 1:18 and Eph 5:23 the intensive nominative pronoun autos (G0846, P-NSM) with the present copula estin (V-PAI-3S). Col 1:18 adds the canon hapax proteuo (G4409, V-PAP-NSM), so that he himself might hold first place, and Col 2:19 makes the head the single source from which the whole body grows. A direct concordance of all 76 kephale occurrences shows kephale and ekklesia co-occur in only three verses, and in all three the head is Christ; the lexeme is never attached to a human over the church. The negative half of the proposition is therefore a sound inference from the singular and intensive grammar plus the empty co-referent slot, not a separate lexeme.

scripture.force: God subjected (hypetaxen, G5293, aorist) all things under his feet and gave him (auton, accusative singular masculine) as head (kephalen, N-ASF) over all things to the church. The church is the recipient of an appointed single head, never a co-head. The accusative kephalen with the singular pronoun fixes one head given to the ekklesia.

Growing up in all things into him who is the head, namely Christ (he kephale, Christos). The head is named explicitly as Christ and is the goal of the body's growth, matching the head-body source language of Col 2:19. No second head is named.

Christ is head (kephale, N-NSF predicate nominative) of the church, he himself savior of the body, set in parallel with the husband as head of the wife. The predicate nominative kephale is anchored to Christos by name, fixing the single referent of the headship over the ekklesia.

And he himself is the head of the body, the church (autos, P-NSM, estin, V-PAI-3S, he kephale, N-NSF), so that in everything he himself might hold first place. The intensive autos plus the canon hapax proteuo (G4409) lexically encodes sole preeminence and leaves no grammatical slot for a shared or human head.

Christ is the head (he kephale) of all rule (arche, G0746) and authority. The same headship lexeme places Christ over every governing power, so the headship language is not a narrow office but a comprehensive supremacy that no created authority shares.

Not holding fast (krateo, G2902) the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and knit together, grows with the growth of God. The head is the single source of supply and cohesion for the body, so failure is defined as not holding the one head rather than choosing among heads.

The man is head of the woman, Christ is head of the man, and God is head of Christ. Here kephale orders persons within a relational chain, showing the lexeme can carry the sense of authority over or alternatively source or origin. This is a different object than the church, and even here the highest head named is God and Christ, never a human over the ekklesia.

complicating_texts.resolution: Here kephale appears in a chain naming the man as head of the woman and God as head of Christ, which shows the lexeme can carry relational ordering and is read by some as authority over and by others as source or origin. This does not weaken the church verses, because the object in Eph and Col is the ekklesia and the body, and a direct concordance shows kephale and ekklesia co-occur in only three verses, all of which name Christ. No human is ever set as head of the church with this lexeme.

The list of apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, and teachers names gifted human roles for equipping the body, but the grammar keeps these as functions given by the ascended Christ, not as kephale of the church. The lexeme kephale is never applied to any of these offices, so they are leaders within the body, a different category than the one head over it, and do not compete with Eph 1:22, Eph 5:23, and Col 1:18.

Here kephale appears in the fixed idiom head of the corner, the cornerstone, also at 1Pet 2:7 and the Synoptic citations of Ps 118. That is a stone metaphor for chief or capstone, a third attested sense of kephale alongside anatomical head and headship of the body. It still lands on Christ and supplies no human head of the church, so it does not disturb the verdict.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied for the Ephesians or Colossians anchors, and the bundle marks these outside published ECM scope, so this is shadow status only. The marked points in the bundle text at Eph 5:23 and Col 1:18 touch word order and the presence of estin, neither of which alters the predication of kephale to Christ over the ekklesia, since the predicate nominative and the intensive autos remain stable.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads kephale in the church verses as ruling authority, so that the singular autos plus singular kephale plus the hapax proteuo fix Christ as the one ruling head with no shared office. The negative half follows directly, because no human is ever named ruling head of the church.

Reads kephale primarily as source or fountainhead, drawing on Col 2:19 where the whole body grows and is supplied from the head. Even on this reading the proposition still holds, because the church is sourced from Christ alone and no human is named as the source from which the body grows. Both attested senses of the word converge on Christ as the single head.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: delegated human leadership within the body
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Notes that elders, overseers, and the gifts of Eph 4:11 lead within the body. Read fairly, this is not a rival to the verdict, because the texts assign these their authority as gifts given by the head and never call any of them kephale of the church. They are leaders within, not the head over, so the single-head claim and ordinary human leadership are different categories that do not conflict.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on the grammar of the head-body metaphor read across Ephesians and Colossians by analogy of Scripture. The one genuine lexical debate, whether kephale means authority over or source, does not move the verdict, because on either sense the head of the church is Christ alone. The negative half of the proposition is inferred from the singular and intensive constructions and the empty co-referent slot.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine how the lexeme kephale is predicated of Christ in relation to the church and the body, and whether the grammar identifies one head or admits an additional or human head.
stem_audit.notes: The stem carries an exclusivity frame in the words alone and no human being holds that office or shares that authority. The positive identification of Christ as kephale of the ekklesia and the body is explicit in Eph 1:22, Eph 4:15, Eph 5:23, Col 1:18, and Col 2:10. The negative exclusion of human headship is an inference from the singular subject, the intensive autos, and a concordance showing kephale and ekklesia co-occur in only three verses, all naming Christ, rather than from a separate lexeme. The verdict was derived on the original stem, and the inference is judged sound because the lexeme is never applied to a human over the church.

lay_summary: Five passages drive this proposition, and they all use the same Greek word for head, kephale. In Ephesians 1:22 God gives Christ as head over all things to the church. In Ephesians 4:15 the head is named plainly as Christ. In Ephesians 5:23 Christ is head of the church, the savior of the body. In Colossians 1:18 he himself is the head of the body, the church, and the rare verb proteuo, which appears only once in the whole canon, says that in everything he himself holds first place. Colossians 2:10 calls him head of all rule and authority, and Colossians 2:19 says the whole body grows only by holding fast to the head, who supplies and knits it together. In each case the subject is singular, the verb is is, and the intensive pronoun autos points back to one person, Christ. A search of all seventy-six places the word head occurs is telling: head and church land in the same verse only three times, and every one of them names Christ. The word is never attached to any human in relation to the church. The positive half of the claim, that Christ is the one head, is therefore stated outright. The negative half, that no human holds or shares the office, follows from the grammar and from that empty slot. There is one honest word-level debate. The word head can mean authority over someone or it can mean source and origin, and 1 Corinthians 11:3 uses it to order persons rather than to describe the church. But on either sense the head of the church is still Christ, and even there the highest head named is God and Christ, never a human. Leaders such as elders and the gifted roles in Ephesians 4 work inside the body and are never called its head, which is a different category. So the lexical pattern strongly supports a single head. The support is dense and grammatically tight but sits within two letters rather than spanning the whole canon, so it is decisive yet local.
